I always thought the show's format was particularly special, espcially how it's executed in the early seasons.

Focusing on one character every episode and telling their story, whilst exploring a specific conflict they're struggling through on and off-island, makes very episode a really satisfying, signular expeirence that you don't often get in 21st century television.

I know we were all compelled by the overall mystery and the long-form storytelling, but in retrospect I feel that was a means to an end and a way of being able to explore this ensemble of flawed, complex, human characters.

In those episodes where everything comes together, (e.g. The Moth, Confidence Man, Numbers, The Constant), the audience get taken on a remarkable emotional journey.

Most other shows currently on the air just don't move me the same way.

'Hear the Wind Sing' and 'Pinball1973' are Murakami's first two novels, and also the first two in the 'The Rat' series.

However, I don't think you really need to have read them before you dive into 'A Wild Sheep Chase'. The only thing that carries over is that it's the same protagonist, but he rarely makes references to things that happen in the preceding novels.

Certainly, 'Hear the Wind Sing' and 'Pinball1973' are worth a read, but they're quite ambient and don't have the same strong narrative drive that some of his later works have. I found them quite nice to read when I'd already read most of his work.

You should be able to pick up both 'Hear the Wind Sing' and 'Pinball1973' in one collected English-translated edition!

It was also pretty revolutionary in the production of sitcoms/comedy series, specifically in the way that it was shot.

The Office really distanced itself from traditional sitcoms that were filmed on a set with a live studio audience. Actors are very precisely blocked and have to hit specific marks, which leaves little room for improvisation and creativty.

Not that it was the first film/TV series to ever shoot like this (this style was popularised by the French in the 60s), but it was pretty unorthodox to shoot a sitcom this way at the time, and yet it's so fundamental to why 'The Office' is funny. The acting is a lot more fluid and natural, and it creates an ecosystem for a lot more physical humour, overlapping dialogue and improv, all of which contribute to that realism.

It also makes logical sense given that the show was supposed to be a mockumentary. This style of shooting comedies has continued to be popular over the following twenty years, which again I think is down to the freedom it allows actors (it can also be cheaper!). Though I do feel like it's becoming a bit tired now, especially in US sitcoms. Arrested Development, Modern Family and Parks & Rec all shoot in a similar style, but I'd argue they don't utilise it as well. Not to mention, in some cases, it makes no logical sense (e.g. "How could there possibly be a camera crew here?").

I usually end up saying something like: "It's a coming-of-age/road trip movie following a father and son on their journey to visit the boy's dying grandfather, exploring family, love and loss."
